event-risk-assessment-proposal-guide.title: The Risk Nobody Quotes: Why Your AV Proposal Ignores the Most Important Part of the Job
event-risk-assessment-proposal-guide.excerpt: Every AV proposal lists equipment and prices. Almost none address the risks that equipment creates — power loads, rigging safety, cable hazards, crowd flow. Here's why risk assessment belongs inside your proposal, not in a separate Word doc.
event-risk-assessment-proposal-guide.author: Sherif Abdalazeem
content: Your proposal says '20 moving heads on a 12m truss.' It does not mention the 480kg load that truss is carrying, whether the venue ceiling can handle it, when the rigging was last inspected, or who is responsible if a safety chain fails. Your proposal says '3-phase power distribution for LED wall and PA.' It does not mention the total amperage draw, whether the venue's supply can handle it without tripping, or what happens when the caterer plugs six chafing dishes into the same circuit. Every AV company in the industry quotes equipment. Almost none of them quote the risks that equipment creates. And that gap — between what you are selling and what could go wrong — is where contracts are lost, incidents happen, and reputations are built or destroyed.

The strange thing is that risk assessment is not optional. In the UK, the Health and Safety Executive requires a written risk assessment for any event involving five or more people. Most countries have equivalent regulations. Event venues increasingly demand risk documentation before allowing load-in. Insurance underwriters want to see it. Yet the AV industry treats risk assessment as an afterthought — a separate Word document pulled from a folder of templates, filled with generic language that has nothing to do with the specific equipment being deployed. The proposal quotes the gear; the risk assessment lives somewhere else entirely. These two documents describe the same job, but they never talk to each other.

This disconnect is not just administrative sloppiness — it is a fundamental design flaw in how AV companies communicate with clients. The equipment list IS the risk source. A 6mm LED wall on ground-supported frames creates different risks than a 3mm wall flown from truss. A wireless microphone system in a venue with heavy RF interference creates different risks than the same system in an RF-clean room. Twelve PAR cans on a 3m tripod stand create a tipping risk that does not exist when those same fixtures are clamped to overhead truss. Separating the equipment list from the risk assessment is like writing a recipe and putting the allergen warnings in a different book. The information belongs together because one directly causes the other.

A proper event risk assessment follows the HSE's 5-step process: identify the hazards, decide who might be harmed and how, evaluate the risks and decide on precautions, record your findings, and review and update. The industry standard tool for evaluation is the 5x5 risk matrix — likelihood scored 1 to 5 multiplied by impact scored 1 to 5, producing a risk score from 1 (trivial) to 25 (catastrophic). What most AV companies miss is the breadth of hazards that AV equipment introduces. Power loads and electrical safety — total amperage draw, circuit capacity, RCD protection, wet-weather protocols for outdoor events. Rigging and structural loading — weight calculations, venue weight limits, safety chains, rigging inspection schedules, wind loading for outdoor structures. Cable management — trip hazards in audience areas, cable ramps for high-traffic zones, overhead cable runs near emergency exits. Weather exposure for outdoor events — rain protection for electronics, wind ratings for LED walls and speaker arrays, temperature limits for projectors and batteries. Crowd flow impact — how AV placement affects emergency egress, whether speaker stacks block fire exits, whether cable runs cross evacuation routes. Working at height — anyone operating above 2m needs fall protection, and the equipment they are installing needs a lifting plan.

How do most AV companies handle risk assessment today? The honest answer: badly. The majority reuse a generic Word document or Excel spreadsheet across every job, changing the event name and date but leaving the same boilerplate hazards and mitigations regardless of whether they are deploying a small PA for a boardroom or rigging 2 tonnes of lighting for an arena show. Some use no risk assessment at all until a client or venue specifically asks for one — and then it is rushed out the day before load-in. Standalone tools like RiskFly exist, but they operate in complete isolation from the proposal. You build your equipment list in one system and your risk assessment in another, with no connection between them. The result is that risk assessments rarely reflect the actual equipment being deployed, mitigations are generic rather than specific, and the document is treated as a compliance checkbox rather than a genuine safety planning tool.

Everything changes when risk assessment is integrated directly into the proposal. First, you catch missing equipment. When you assess a cable run across a public walkway, you realize you have not quoted cable ramps. When you evaluate rigging loads, you notice you have not included safety chains or a backup motor. When you assess power distribution, you spot that you need an RCD unit that was not in the original equipment list. The risk assessment becomes a quality check on the proposal itself — every hazard identified is an opportunity to add the safety equipment that prevents it, and that equipment gets priced into the quote rather than becoming a surprise cost on event day.

Second, integrated risk assessment transforms how clients perceive your proposal. When a corporate event manager receives two proposals for the same conference — one is a bare equipment list with a total at the bottom, the other includes a detailed risk assessment with specific hazards, scored risks, named mitigation measures, and a responsible person for each — the second proposal wins on trust before anyone compares prices. The risk assessment signals that you have thought beyond 'what equipment do we need' to 'what could go wrong and how do we prevent it.' For clients in regulated industries — pharmaceutical conferences, financial services events, government functions — this is not a differentiator, it is a requirement. And even for clients who do not require it, seeing a risk plan built into the proposal elevates your company from 'AV vendor' to 'production partner.'

Third, you become HSE-compliant from the moment the proposal is accepted. There is no scramble to produce a separate risk assessment document before load-in. There is no risk of the assessment contradicting the equipment list because they were written at different times by different people. The proposal IS the safety plan. When the venue asks for your risk documentation, you send the same PDF the client already approved. One document, one source of truth, one less thing that can fall through the cracks on a busy production schedule.

CueQuote is the only AV proposal platform that integrates risk assessment directly into the proposal workflow. Every proposal includes a Risk Assessment tab alongside Equipment, Terms, and Comments. Each hazard is scored on a 5x5 matrix — likelihood from 1 (rare) to 5 (almost certain) multiplied by impact from 1 (negligible) to 5 (catastrophic) — producing an auto-calculated risk score with color-coded severity. For each hazard, you record the mitigation measure and the responsible person. When you export the proposal to PDF, you can include the risk assessment as a dedicated section — your client receives an equipment list, pricing, terms, and a professional safety plan in a single branded document. Your competitors send a quote. You send a proposal with a safety plan built in. For a deeper look at how CueQuote handles risk categories and AI-generated risk plans, read our guide on risk assessment in AV events.

The AV industry has spent years competing on equipment specs and price. The companies that will win the next decade of contracts are the ones that compete on trust, professionalism, and operational maturity. Integrating risk assessment into your proposals is one of the highest-impact, lowest-effort ways to demonstrate all three. Stop sending equipment lists and start sending production plans. Try CueQuote free — your first proposal with a built-in risk assessment takes less than five minutes.

av-cost-london-corporate-events.title: What Does AV Cost for a Corporate Event in London? A 2026 Guide
av-cost-london-corporate-events.excerpt: London runs 25–30% above other major UK cities for corporate events — but the premium is not where most planners look for it. The equipment is close to national rates. The extra money goes on crew, venue commissions, rigging and access.
content: Ask three London production companies to quote the same conference and you can easily see a spread of two to one. That is not because one of them is dishonest. It is because London budgets contain a set of costs that never appear on a regional quote at all, and different companies make different assumptions about who is absorbing them. Industry figures put London corporate events roughly 25 to 30 percent above equivalent events in other major UK cities. This guide breaks down where that money actually goes in 2026, because the answer is not the one most planners expect.

Start with the surprise: the equipment is not the expensive part. Hire rates for kit are fairly national. LED screen hire in London runs from about £250 a day for a small panel setup to £4,000 or more for a large high-specification wall, and a popular conference size of roughly 6 by 3 metres typically totals £3,500 to £6,000 per day including the panels, processor, support structure, delivery and a standard crew day. Audio follows the same pattern — a simple speaker-and-microphone package starts near £50, while a full conference PA runs to £700 or more per day. A small conference with a projector and a PA can start around £500; add LED screens and a live stream and you are past £2,000. Those are numbers a supplier in Leeds would recognise.

The first genuine London premium is labour. UK technician day rates sit between £350 and £650, and London consistently occupies the upper half of that band, with specialists — audio engineers, lighting designers, video engineers — above it. The London premium here is not only the headline rate. It is that crew days in central London are less efficient: a get-in that would take four hours in a regional exhibition hall takes six in a listed building with a single service lift, and you are paying for the difference. When you compare two quotes, check the number of crew days before you check the rate.

The second, and the one that catches out planners new to London venues, is the venue's own commercial arrangement. A large share of London corporate venues either operate an in-house AV supplier or hold an exclusive supplier list. Where an outside company is permitted at all, venues commonly levy an outside vendor fee — also called a patch fee or preferred supplier charge — of 20 to 40 percent of the AV value. Where you use the in-house supplier instead, venue commissions of 30 to 50 percent are typically built into the pricing you are quoted. Either way the venue is taking a share. The question is only whether you can see it on the invoice.

The third is rigging, and London's venue stock makes it unavoidable more often than elsewhere. Anything suspended above an audience — lighting bars, projection, LED, truss — triggers a structural process: an engineering assessment to confirm load capacity, certified riggers to install and strike, and liability insurance for the suspended elements. Many venues require you to use their own rigging contractor, which removes your ability to shop the price. Some charge per hanging point, others bill the rigging crew hourly. For a corporate gala or awards ceremony with overhead lighting and projection, rigging alone commonly adds a four-figure sum before a single fixture is switched on.

The fourth is access, and it is the one that never appears as a line item. Central London get-ins are constrained by loading bay availability, narrow delivery windows agreed with the venue, restricted vehicle access on surrounding streets, and the city's emission and congestion charging schemes, which apply to production vehicles like any other. The practical consequence is that a job which needs one van in Birmingham may need two smaller vehicles and an extra crew member in Soho, or an overnight get-in at premium rates because the only available window is between midnight and six. Ask any prospective supplier what get-in window the venue has offered before you accept their crew estimate.

Then there are the charges that sit outside the AV quote but inside your budget. VAT at 20 percent applies. Venues typically add a service charge of 12.5 to 15 percent on food and beverage, along with separate charges for power distribution, internet bandwidth, security, and overtime beyond agreed hours. Taken together, the charges that are not in the headline AV number commonly add 30 to 50 percent to what a planner first budgets. This is the single largest source of unpleasant surprises in London event budgeting, and it is entirely predictable if you ask for the venue's full schedule of technical charges before you sign.

So what should you actually expect to spend? For a 50 to 80 person meeting in a London hotel with a projector, screen, two microphones and a modest PA, budget in the region of £1,200 to £2,800 for the AV itself, before venue technical charges. For a 200 person conference with a proper PA, an LED backdrop, six microphones, stage lighting and a two-person crew, £4,500 to £11,000 is a realistic band. For a 300 to 500 person gala or awards evening with an LED wall, moving-head lighting, multi-camera coverage and a full crew, expect £14,000 to £32,000. Every one of those figures assumes you are not paying an outside vendor penalty, and none of them includes venue charges, rigging fees or content production.

When you receive a London quote, three checks will tell you most of what you need to know. First, does it state the number of crew and the number of crew days, or only a total? A quote that hides crew days is a quote that can grow on the day. Second, does it name who is rigging, and whether the venue mandates its own contractor? Third, does it say explicitly what is excluded — power, rigging, venue fees, content, transport? The cheapest quote in a London tender is very often the one with the narrowest scope, and the difference reappears as change orders during the get-in, when you have no leverage left.

If you want a starting figure before you approach suppliers, our AV cost calculator will give you an itemised range for your headcount and production spec in a few seconds, and our 2026 price guide lists the underlying day rates. If you are on the other side of the table and it is you writing the quote, CueQuote builds a priced proposal from your own catalogue and your own rates in under two minutes.

av-cost-dubai-uae-events.title: What Does AV Cost for a Corporate Event in Dubai? A 2026 Guide
av-cost-dubai-uae-events.excerpt: Dubai AV pricing is competitive by international standards — a conference audio rig runs AED 1,200 to 3,500 a day. What decides your budget is the calendar and the venue minimum spend, not the equipment list.
content: Dubai is one of the easier markets in the world to hire AV in, and one of the harder ones to budget for. Equipment is plentiful, competition between rental houses is real, and day rates compare well internationally. What catches planners out is that the two largest variables in a Dubai event budget are not on the AV quote at all: when in the year you hold it, and what the venue requires you to spend before you hire a single speaker.

Start with the equipment, because it is the reassuring part. A basic PA suitable for up to 50 attendees runs about AED 300 to 800 per day. A conference audio rig for 50 to 300 attendees — a PA with subwoofers, monitors and a wireless microphone package — sits between AED 1,200 and AED 3,500 per day. Premium configurations for larger rooms run AED 3,000 to AED 8,000. LED screens start around AED 1,600 including delivery for panel sizes in the 115 to 300 inch range. VAT is 5 percent, a fraction of what European planners are used to budgeting.

The thing that will move your number more than any equipment choice is the season. Dubai's event calendar is compressed into roughly October to April, when the weather makes outdoor and semi-outdoor formats viable and the international conference circuit is in town. Inside that window, good crews and the better inventory book out early and price accordingly. Outside it, in deep summer, you will find availability and negotiating room, but most corporate formats move indoors entirely and the venue options narrow. If your date is flexible by even a fortnight, ask what that fortnight is worth before you fix it.

The second is the venue's commercial floor. A five-star hotel ballroom in Dubai typically carries a hire fee plus a minimum spend that can reach AED 150,000 to AED 250,000 before any food or beverage is ordered, let alone production. For many corporate events this single number dominates the budget so completely that the AV specification becomes a rounding error beside it. The practical consequence is that venue selection, not equipment selection, is where your budget is actually decided — model two or three venues fully before committing, rather than optimising an AV quote against a venue you have already signed.

Full production for a gala — lighting design, audio, LED walls, projection mapping, staging and a technical crew — commonly lands between AED 50,000 and AED 150,000 as a standalone line. That is a wide band, and where you fall in it is driven mostly by the LED specification and the ambition of the lighting design rather than by headcount. Crew rates in the Middle East are broadly comparable to United States pricing, so a full technical team is a substantial part of that figure and should be itemised in any quote you take seriously.

Two Dubai-specific mechanics are worth knowing, because they are levers rather than fixed costs. First, bundling: hiring audio, video, lighting and crew as one package from a single supplier commonly saves 20 to 35 percent against renting each element separately, and it removes the coordination risk of several companies arriving at one loading bay. Second, geography: delivery is often free within the central zones but can add AED 500 or more for venues out towards Al Ain or Fujairah. If your event is outside the city, ask whether transport and crew travel sit inside the quoted price or outside it.

So what should you expect? For a 50 to 100 person meeting in a hotel with a projector, screen, microphones and a modest PA, AED 3,000 to AED 8,000 for the AV is a realistic band. For a 200 to 300 person conference with a proper PA, LED, stage lighting and a small crew, AED 15,000 to AED 45,000. For a gala or awards evening with full production, the AED 50,000 to AED 150,000 range above applies. None of these figures includes the venue's hire fee or minimum spend, which will very often be the larger number.

When you compare Dubai quotes, check three things. Does the quote state crew numbers and days separately from equipment, or roll them into a package price you cannot interrogate? Does it include delivery, installation and de-rig, or are those quoted on application? And is it valid across your date, or only outside peak season? av-cost-warsaw-poland-events.title: What Does AV Cost for a Corporate Event in Warsaw? A 2026 Guide
av-cost-warsaw-poland-events.excerpt: Warsaw is Poland's most expensive AV market, and the reason is logistics rather than greed. Here are real 2026 day rates in złoty, plus the two discounts most planners never ask for.
content: Poland has one of the better value event production markets in Europe, and Warsaw is the most expensive part of it. That is not a margin story. Suppliers consistently attribute the Warsaw premium to logistics and parking in the city centre — the same rig costs more to deliver, unload and crew in central Warsaw than in Kraków or Poznań. Understanding where the money goes makes it much easier to see which parts of a quote are negotiable and which are simply the cost of working in the capital.

Audio is the most predictable line. A sound package with an operator for a room of up to about 150 people runs around 2,900 PLN net. Step up to roughly 300 people with stage monitors and you are at about 3,900 PLN net. Across the market, sound hire runs from about 800 PLN a day for a basic set to 15,000 PLN for a professional line array serving 1,000 people or more, depending on system power, the number of wireless microphones, the quality of the console, and whether an operator is included. Audio typically accounts for 18 to 25 percent of a total technical budget.

LED is where Warsaw's premium is most visible. A P2.6 screen at 3 by 2 metres — a standard conference and gala size — runs 3,500 to 5,000 PLN per day. The finer P1.9 pitch in the same size costs 4,500 to 7,000 PLN. A larger 12 square metre screen at 4 by 3 metres comes in around 8,500 PLN per day including installation and crew. As a rule of thumb, Warsaw pricing works out near 400 PLN per square metre per day, and indoor LED hire in the capital is openly priced above other Polish cities for the logistics reasons above.

Labour is the largest single component and the one most often underestimated: across Polish technical production, crew accounts for 30 to 50 percent of the total. That ratio is worth holding in your head when you read a quote, because it is a fast credibility check. A quote where equipment dominates and crew is a small afterthought is usually a quote that has not fully scoped the setup, the operation and the strike. For scale, a large gala production can field a dozen technicians plus two directors, with the team cost alone reaching tens of thousands of złoty.

Two discounts exist in this market and most planners never ask for either. The first is multi-day: suppliers commonly apply around 15 percent off the second day and 25 percent off the third and subsequent days, because the expensive parts — transport, load-in, load-out — happen once regardless of how long you keep the kit. If your event is two days, the second day should not cost the same as the first, and if a quote prices it as though it does, ask why. The second is timing, which works against you rather than for you: weekend dates in May and gala season in December commonly carry a 20 to 30 percent premium. Moving a date by a week inside those periods can be worth more than any equipment substitution.

If your event is hybrid or streamed, budget it as a separate production rather than an add-on. An online conference for 200 to 500 participants with two or three cameras, a video mixer, encoding, a streaming platform and an on-site technician runs 12,000 to 18,000 PLN for a full day. That is a meaningful line next to the in-room technical budget, and it is the item most likely to be quoted vaguely, because the platform, the encoding and the operator are easy to leave implied.

Two more things belong in a Polish budget that are not in the AV quote. VAT is 23 percent, and quotes from technical suppliers are conventionally given net, so the number you are reading is not the number you will pay. And venue technical conditions — available power, load-in access, rigging permissions, get-in windows — vary enormously between a purpose-built conference centre and a historic building, and they drive crew hours more than any equipment decision does. Ask the venue for its technical specification before you brief suppliers, not after.

If you are the one writing the quote rather than receiving it, CueQuote builds a priced proposal from your own catalogue and your own rates in under two minutes.

cuequote-v134-whats-new.title: What's New in CueQuote 1.34
cuequote-v134-whats-new.excerpt: Start a proposal straight from the AV cost calculator, and pricing that finally tells equipment and crew apart market by market.
content: Version 1.34 does two things: it connects the AV cost calculator on our website to the app, and it fixes how we price events in different markets. The second one is the bigger change, and it is worth explaining why.

Start a proposal from the calculator. Until now, if you priced an event on our AV cost calculator and then signed up, everything you had configured was thrown away and you landed on an empty form. Now your configuration carries across. Pick the country your event is in, set the attendee count and days, choose your video, lighting and staging — then click through, and your first proposal opens already filled in with the event you just priced. The estimate stays what it always was, orientation rather than a quote: CueQuote re-prices everything from your own catalogue and your own rates before anything reaches a client.
The calculator now covers 66 markets, shows prices in local currency at exchange rates refreshed daily, and breaks the estimate down line by line rather than showing a single number.

Pricing that tells equipment and crew apart. We used to apply one multiplier per region to everything — equipment, crew, catering, decor. That turns out to be wrong in a way that matters. Professional AV hardware is bought on a single global market: a line array or an LED panel costs roughly the same to buy in Warsaw as in Munich, so its rental price barely moves between countries. Crew is entirely local, and varies enormously. One number cannot describe both.

We audited published rate cards across thirteen regions to find out how far off we were. Japan made the problem obvious — equipment there prices above the Western European baseline while a technician costs about a third of it. The Gulf was the largest error: our 2.5x multiplier turned out to match what Dubai hotels charge for in-house AV, not what the open rental market charges, which sits below parity. Gulf events were being estimated at roughly three times reality.

Every region now carries two multipliers, one for equipment and one for crew and locally-produced services. Planners in the Gulf, the United States, Eastern Europe and East Asia will see the biggest change. Where the research found nothing citable — Egypt, India, Latin America and Africa — we left the existing values alone and recorded in the code that they are unverified, rather than replacing a guess with a better-dressed guess.

rentman-alternative-small-av-companies.title: Rentman Alternative for Small AV Companies
rentman-alternative-small-av-companies.excerpt: Rentman is excellent operations software — and priced per user. If your bottleneck is quoting rather than warehouse chaos, here is how to decide honestly.
content: If you run a small AV company — one to five people — and you are weighing up Rentman, the honest starting point is that Rentman is very good software, and probably more software than you need today. It is built to solve the operational problem of a rental business at scale: where every case of equipment is, who has it, when it comes back, and what it is worth. If that is your daily pain, stop reading and go buy it. This article is for the smaller operator whose actual bottleneck sits somewhere else.

Rentman earned its position in the European AV market by taking equipment operations seriously. Barcode and QR tracking on individual assets, warehouse workflows, crew scheduling, subhire management, availability across overlapping jobs — these are genuinely hard problems and Rentman solves them properly. For a company running a warehouse of thousands of items and a crew of twenty, that infrastructure pays for itself quickly, and there is no serious argument for replacing it.

The friction for small teams is the pricing model rather than the product. Rentman charges a 39 euro monthly platform fee, then modules on top of it per power user: Inventory from 14 euros, Crew from 14, and Quoting and Invoicing as a 9 euro add-on (checked August 2026). For a three-person company that is somewhere between 42 and 117 euros a month; for five people, 70 to 195. That is fair value for warehouse infrastructure — but you pay it per seat whether or not the person in that seat ever touches the warehouse features.

So the question that actually decides this is not which platform is better. It is which bottleneck is costing you more money this quarter. If jobs go out with missing gear, if you double-book equipment, if you cannot say what is in the van without walking to it — that is an operations problem and you need operations software. If your inventory fits in your head and your real problem is that quoting a job takes three hours you do not have, that is a proposal problem, and operations software will not fix it.

Small AV companies lose more deals to proposal latency than to warehouse chaos. The client emails on Tuesday, three suppliers get asked, and whoever answers first with something that looks professional shapes the decision. If you are quoting in the evening after site visits, you are routinely the third response — and by then the brief has been anchored by somebody else's document.

A proposal-first alternative attacks that specific problem. CueQuote is flat-rate rather than per user — 29 euros a month for Starter, 79 for Pro, excluding VAT — and the core of it is that you describe the event in plain language and get back a structured equipment list, priced from your own catalogue, in a couple of minutes rather than a couple of hours. Everything after that is editing rather than authoring, which is a fundamentally cheaper task.

For a three-person company the arithmetic is stark. Rentman across three power users runs from about 81 euros a month — the 39 euro platform fee plus three Inventory seats — and around 156 with quoting and the Pro tiers. CueQuote Starter is 29 euros a month for the company rather than the seat, and Pro is 79. If only one or two people ever write proposals, per-seat pricing charges you for a shape of business you do not have yet.

Be clear about what you give up. CueQuote does not track equipment with barcodes, does not manage a warehouse, does not schedule crew across overlapping jobs, and does not handle subhire. If you need those things you need Rentman or something like it, and no amount of proposal speed compensates. Choosing a proposal-first tool is a statement that your inventory is still small enough to manage without software — true for a lot of small AV companies, and it stops being true as you grow.

The two are not mutually exclusive either. Plenty of companies run operations software for the warehouse and something faster at the front end, because the tools optimise for different moments in the job. The expensive mistake is paying for a full operations platform per seat and then still writing proposals by hand in a word processor — that is the worst of both.

The practical way to decide takes about a week. Count the proposals you sent last month and the hours they took. Count the jobs where equipment problems cost you money. Whichever number is bigger is the software you should buy first. Both platforms have free entry points, so this is a question you can answer with evidence rather than opinion. If you have already decided Rentman is not the fit and want the short version, here is a Rentman alternative for AV quoting.

cuequote-integrations-api-widget-webhook.title: CueQuote Now Connects to Your Website, CRM and AI
cuequote-integrations-api-widget-webhook.excerpt: Four new ways to connect CueQuote: an instant quote form for your site, a REST API, webhooks into your CRM, and an MCP server for AI assistants.
content: Until now, CueQuote was somewhere you went. You opened the app, described an event, and got a proposal back. That is still the centre of it — but it left an obvious gap: the quote lived in CueQuote and nowhere else. This release closes that gap in four directions: your website, your own systems, your CRM, and your AI assistant.

An instant quote form for your website. Most AV company websites end at “contact us for a quote”. The visitor fills in a form, waits two or three days, and in the meantime asks two of your competitors as well. The new website quote form replaces that with a real number while they are still reading your page.
[IMAGE:/blog/widget-form.png|The form as a visitor sees it — one script tag, no iframe, no build step.]

Installation is a single script tag. Paste it into WordPress, Squarespace, Wix, Webflow or plain HTML and the form renders where you put it. It runs inside an isolated shadow root, so your site's CSS cannot break the form and the form cannot break your layout.
The visitor describes their event, adds a guest count and their contact details, and gets a budget range broken down by category — audio, lighting, video, staging, crew.
[IMAGE:/blog/widget-estimate.png|The estimate: a total range and a category breakdown, priced from the company's own catalogue. Unit prices are never shown.]

What matters most here is what the visitor does not see. No unit prices, no equipment list, no line items — only ranges, and clearly labelled as indicative rather than as a quote. Your rate card is the thing that makes the estimate accurate, and it is also the thing you would never publish. It stays on our side of the line, which is what makes this safe to put on a public page a competitor can read.

What you get is considerably better than a contact form: an email with the enquiry and, waiting in CueQuote, a fully costed draft proposal at your real prices, with the client already created and attached. The slow part of answering an enquiry is finished before you have read the email.

A REST API. If you would rather drive CueQuote from your own systems, POST an event description to /v1/proposals and get a costed proposal back as JSON — total, line items and a share link. Create a key in Settings, send it as a bearer token, and that is the entire integration. Full reference in the API docs.

Webhooks. Polling an API to find out whether a client accepted is both wasteful and slow. Add an endpoint instead, and we post a signed payload the moment a proposal is sent, viewed, accepted or rejected. Every delivery is signed with HMAC-SHA256 so you can prove it came from us and not from anyone who learned your URL. Settings shows delivery counts and flags an endpoint that has stopped responding — because a CRM integration that quietly breaks otherwise tells nobody, and proposals simply stop arriving.

An MCP server. Connect CueQuote to Claude, ChatGPT or any assistant that speaks Model Context Protocol, then ask in plain language: “Quote the Warsaw conference — 300 people, keynote stage with LED, four breakout rooms, 14 October.” It answers from your own equipment catalogue and saves a draft. It is not guessing at prices; it is calling your account.

All four run the same estimator. This matters more than it sounds. A quote produced by the form on your website, by the API from your CRM, by an assistant, or by you in the app is the same quote — same catalogue, same regional pricing, same rules. There is no second, worse pricing engine hiding behind the integrations.

None of them can send anything to a client. Everything the integrations create is a draft. Sending stays a deliberate act you take in the app after reviewing what was generated, which is exactly where that decision belongs when a machine wrote the first version.

The website quote form is available on Pro and above. The API, webhooks and the MCP server are on Business. All four are documented with working code: website quote form, API, webhooks and MCP. If you are building something we have not covered, tell us — we would rather hear about it early.

sub-hire-work-orders-without-sharing-you.title: Sub Work Out Without Handing Over Your Client
sub-hire-work-orders-without-sharing-you.excerpt: Send a dry-hire house their scope, their price and the load-in window on one link — and nothing about the client you spent years winning.
content: Almost every AV job has a part someone else does. A dry-hire house covers the boxes you are short of, a rigger comes in for the day, a caterer takes the whole hospitality line. The work is routine. What you send them usually is not: a forwarded PDF with the prices still in it, or an email trimmed by hand at seven in the morning, hoping you deleted the right lines.

The risk in that is not really the price. It is the client. A proposal names them on every page, and a supplier who learns who the end client is has everything they need to quote that client directly next year. A non-solicitation clause is worth very little if the document it sits on names the company it is meant to protect.

CueQuote now issues a work order instead. Open the Suppliers tab on any job, tick the lines you are subbing out — or, in Planner mode, award a whole section such as Catering — and send one link. This is what the supplier opens, with no login and no account:
[IMAGE:/blog/work-order-supplier-view.png|A work order as the supplier sees it: their scope, the venue, the load-in window, the site contact, and their own price. No client name, no sell price.]

Everything they need to turn up and work is there: what they are supplying, the dates, the venue and address, the load-in window, and who to call on site. The total reads GBP 2,466 — what this supplier is being paid. On the job it came from, those same three lines are sold for GBP 5,840. The supplier never sees that number, and never sees the client's name, contact details or the proposal's scope summary.

The scope text is written from the lines you selected rather than copied from the proposal. That is not a stylistic choice. A proposal's scope summary is written for the client and names them — "full-service production for Halstead Financial's annual results briefing" — so it can never be forwarded. Generating the text from the items also describes the job more usefully: what the supplier is supplying, not what the event is about.

The part that is easy to miss is item descriptions. Those are written for the client too, and they get copied onto the order. So CueQuote reads them, and refuses to issue a work order whose text names your client — pointing at the line to fix, even when it is a line you did not write. If a flagged word is ordinary vocabulary for you rather than a client's identity, you mark it once for that client and it is never flagged again.

Insurance is checked, and checked against the right date. Add a supplier's public liability expiry once, and a work order will not go out if the cover runs out before your load-out — not merely if it has already lapsed today. Cover that is valid the week you book and expired on the morning of the show is the failure that actually costs money, and checking against today waves it straight through. You can still send: the reason goes on the order with your name against it, which is the point of an override rather than a block.

The supplier accepts by typing their name. The date, the time and their answer are recorded on the order, so "they confirmed on the 3rd" stops being a memory of a phone call. If the job changes, or the link gets forwarded to someone it should not reach, revoke it. Reading and accepting stop together — a revoked link that could still confirm a booking would be worse than one that could still read a venue name.
[IMAGE:/blog/work-order-revoked.png|A revoked link. A wrong token, an expired one and a withdrawn one all say the same thing, so nobody can tell which they hold.]

Planner mode works the same way with a different unit. An organiser rarely subs out three line items; they award Catering, or Production, or Transport, to one supplier in one go. Pick the section and the scope text writes itself from everything under it.

It is available on every plan. Free accounts keep two work orders live at a time, Starter ten, and Pro and above unlimited — and revoking one frees the slot, so the limit is about what is outstanding rather than what you have ever sent.
